Right: without the edge a-z, drawn dashed, the nodes z, b, x, a form an induced path on four nodes, in the accent color, so is_cograph() returns False." width="100%"} A *cograph* (complement-reducible graph) can be built from single nodes by taking disjoint unions and joins, where a join adds every edge between two graphs. Equivalently, it has no induced path on four nodes (no $P_4$), and its modular decomposition (see `modular_decomposition()`) has no prime nodes: every module with more than one node is disconnected or has a disconnected complement. The tree then describes the graph completely, which makes many hard problems (cliques, coloring, independent sets, Hamiltonicity) easy on cographs. Self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : `True` if the graph is a cograph. The empty graph and a single node are. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~modular_decomposition`) : The tree whose prime nodes this checks for. ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The graph is a cograph exactly when its modular decomposition has no prime node (Corneil, Lerchs and Stewart Burlingham, 1981), so this runs `modular_decomposition()` and stops short of building the tree. Linear-time cograph recognizers exist; this shares the decomposition's cost instead. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A complete bipartite graph is the join of two edgeless graphs, so it is a cograph. Dropping the edge a-z leaves z, b, x, a as an induced path on four nodes, and the graph is no longer one: ::: {#accc90eb .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["a", "b", "x", "y", "z"]) g.add_edges([(u, v) for u in "ab" for v in "xyz"]) before = g.is_cograph() g.delete_edge("a", "z") before, g.is_cograph() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (True, False) ``` ::: :::
